transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Kievone.
More than 54 million people have already voted early
in the midterm elections, according to the University
of Florida's election lab.
NPR's Tamara Keith looks
at the current political environment.
>> This election season started out on favorable ground
for Republicans, between a Senate map that runs
through red states and all the gerrymandering
of House districts, but voters are unhappy.
The average price of regular gasoline is over $4 a gallon.
Inflation is up.
People are worried about artificial intelligence
and data centers.
The war with Iran is unpopular,
and voters are increasingly voicing concerns
about corruption.
Senate races in deep red Republican territory are
competitive, as are House districts
where President Trump won by 10 points
or more just two years ago.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
>> Democratic Congresswoman Hayley Stevens is revoking her
endorsement of her former primary rival
in the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed,
now backing his Republican opponent,
former Congressman Mike Rogers.
NPR's Sam Gringless has details.
>> Stevens has been criticizing El-Sayed for not doing enough
to win over many black and Jewish voters
who backed her in the primary.
After trading seething statements in recent days,
a planned joint appearance at a church in Detroit fell apart.
El-Sayed spoke to reporters outside that event,
which went on without her.
>> None of this matters.
You know what matters?
There's a family.
You can go like 15 minutes that way or 15 minutes that way
or 15 minutes that way, and there are families
who are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow
that look like they did 50 years ago.
They're worried about what they're going
to feed their kids for lunch.
They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick,
they're not going to be able to pay the bills.
Those are the things that matter.
>> Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer
called Stevens' reversal a despicable betrayal.
Holding the Michigan Senate seat is key for Democrats
to retake the chamber.
Sam Gringless, NPR News, Detroit.
>> The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments this week
in a case that pits the Catholic Church
against taxpayer-funded school programs
for all 4-year-olds in Colorado.
NPR's Nina Totenberg reports.
>> The first line of the Bill of Rights says Congress
shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion
or prohibiting the free exercise of religion.
But what happens when these two provisions clash?
In this week's case, the question
is whether a taxpayer-funded program
that provides pre-K schooling for all 4-year-olds
in the state must include a religious group --
in this case, the Catholic Archdiocese of Denver --
which bars the children of gay and trans parents
from the pre-K program.
If the church prevails, the next target
is likely to be charter schools.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
>> This is NPR News in Washington.
A Learjet carrying nine people crashed into a neighborhood
in South Florida early this afternoon.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy
says all nine people on board have died,
and a federal investigation is underway.
The FAA says the aircraft had departed Austin-Burgstrom Airport
in Texas and was headed for the Bahamas.
Police in central Illinois are investigating
a shooting near a university campus.
One person was killed, seven others were injured.
Eric Stock from member station WGLT reports.
>> The shooting happened early in the morning
near Illinois Wesleyan University in Bloomington,
two hours south of Chicago.
Bloomington police say a 19-year-old woman
was pronounced dead at the scene.
At least three college students were among the wounded.
Police have not made any arrests
and are asking the public to provide any evidence
that may help them identify the shooter.
Kaylin Patterson lives near the scene of the shooting.
>> I feel sad for the victims.
I feel sad for the world and what's happening in the world
and how easy it is to cause harm and violence now.
>> It's the second mass shooting near a college campus
in the community this year.
For NPR News, I'm Eric Stock in Bloomington, Illinois.
>> Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney
is saying he had constructive talks with President Trump
today about a potential trade deal.
Trade friction between the U.S. and Canada
has been a political issue for some states,
especially Michigan and Maine.
The fresh momentum is a turnaround
from a stalemate over the summer.
I'm Louise Schiavone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Midterm early voting tops 54 million, with voters unhappy over gas prices, inflation, and the Iran war
Democrat Hayley Stevens revokes endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed, backs Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
Supreme Court to hear case pitting Catholic Archdiocese of Denver against Colorado's universal pre-K program
Learjet carrying nine crashes into South Florida neighborhood; all nine aboard killed, federal probe underway
Shooting near Illinois Wesleyan University in Bloomington kills one 19-year-old woman, injures seven
Prime Minister Mark Carney reports constructive trade talks with President Trump on a potential deal
